rv.q: But it has a grace that overrides these flaws and it is distinguished by two subtle, moving performances.
But what makes the play so absorbing is that Kani draws us into the lives of the two individuals living out their lives in front of us.
To see these two veteran actors together is a treat.
But even if 'Kunene and the King' is predictable in its shape and story arc, and feels a mite old-fashioned, it's a good-hearted 90 minutes.
Kunene and the King fits into the latter category... a compelling if cursory exploration of the legacy of Apartheid.
It feels like theatre by old people, for old people.
Kani, meanwhile, is simply magnificent in standing his ground against the bullying figure of his patient; this is one of the most tender, beautiful performances currently on the London stage.
Janice Honeyman has had great good fortune in getting an opportunity to direct two of the best actors of their generation and everyone delivers to perfection.
This terrific two-hander is currently berthed at the smallish Ambassadors. It belongs at the National.
Kunene and the King is made remarkably light on its feet by the plain human engagement of these two combatants who, by the end, appear as much apposite as opposite.
Kani's script is entertaining throughout, even if some elements seem occasionally pat: some of the verbal squabbling is stretched.
I wanted to like it more than I did, but I kept being thrown by the fact that at one moment the two were at each other's throats...and the next they were laughing at each other's fallibilities.
The final scene in Kuni's house is a masterclass of pathos and physical comedy as they assert and seal their mutual respect and affection.
Yet for all this preachy, message-laden dialogue, I liked it.
